title: The Most Expensive Trait in Business and Maybe Life in General
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Mulder names laziness as the trait she cannot tolerate, then immediately narrows the definition so the argument does not collapse into hustle moralising. Burnout, exhaustion, grief and mental health are explicitly excluded; what she means is the disguised version that looks like work. Her examples are precise: rewriting the to-do list instead of making decisions, using meetings to vent rather than solve, researching endlessly to postpone executing, and invoking overwhelm when the real deficit is clarity and commitment. This kind of avoidance is characterised as movement rather than momentum, performance rather than progress, and ultimately fear in a sneaky outfit. The cost she identifies is not wasted time but eroded self-trust, because the person avoiding always knows which action would move the needle. She proposes ownership rather than hustle as the true opposite of laziness, defined as doing the one thing that makes everything else irrelevant even when it might fail. The piece ends by turning the test on herself, with an admission that she has delayed starting YouTube not from lack of material but because being seen unpolished is uncomfortable.
points: The definitional work is what saves the argument: by excluding burnout and grief up front, Mulder isolates avoidance that mimics productivity rather than condemning tiredness.
Her four examples of disguised laziness are diagnostic rather than rhetorical, each pairing a productive-looking behaviour with the decision it postpones.
Framing the real cost as eroded self-trust rather than lost time explains why the pattern compounds, since each avoidance confirms you cannot rely on yourself.
Naming ownership rather than hustle as laziness's opposite keeps the remedy about decisions and commitment rather than hours worked.
Mulder's test for whether you are tired or avoiding is circling the same problem week after week while calling it strategy.
quotes: I’ve been there. I know what survival mode looks like. That’s not laziness, that’s life trying to keep you safe.
But it’s movement, not momentum. It’s performance over progress. And it’s fear, in a very sneaky outfit.
The real cost of this kind of laziness isn’t wasted time. It’s the erosion of self-trust.
You know which action would actually move the needle and you’re choosing everything but that.
Because I’ve watched it kill ideas, dreams, and businesses that had everything else going for them. Not because people weren’t talented. But because they wouldn’t act on what mattered most.
The opposite of laziness isn’t hustle. It’s ownership. It’s doing the one thing that makes everything else irrelevant even if it’s scary, even if it’s uncomfortable, even if you might fail.
But if you’re circling the same problem week after week and calling it “strategy,” you’re not tired. You’re avoiding the thing that would change everything.
